subtitle: People with disabilities face real barriers in substance use treatment. Recognize them, help people reach accessible care in Minnesota’s system, and bring harm reduction and stigma-free practice into disability services work.
audience: For case managers and care coordinators, lead agency staff, 245D provider oversight staff, and DSD program, policy and supervisory staff who support or make decisions affecting people with disabilities who use alcohol or other drugs.

lessons.title: Why co-occurring substance use deserves attention
objectives: Describe what federal guidance says about substance use disorders among people with physical and cognitive disabilities.
Identify common barriers that keep people with disabilities out of substance use treatment.
Explain how invisible and cognitive disabilities can be mistaken for poor motivation.
Compare a disability-aware response with a system response that passes the person between departments.
lessons.teaching:
A 2019 advisory comes from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, or SAMHSA. It reports higher rates of serious mental illness and substance use disorders among people with physical and cognitive disabilities. It also reports lower treatment rates for both conditions than among people without these disabilities. The advisory notes several paths into substance use: some people begin using to cope with chronic pain, isolation, stigma or trauma, including physical or sexual abuse. Unemployment and impulsivity are also risk factors. For others, substance use came first and contributed to the injury that caused a disability.

The advisory also identifies barriers within treatment programs. Parking, entrances and rooms may be inaccessible. A rule requiring clients to evacuate a building without help can exclude people with disabilities. Counseling may not meet cognitive access needs. Materials may lack Braille, large-print or electronic versions. Staff may not know how to communicate with people who are deaf. It also describes departments passing responsibility back and forth. Disability departments may turn away people with serious mental illness, while mental health departments turn away people with disabilities. Providers may also overestimate how accessible they are.

Some disabilities are not obvious. SAMHSA cautions that behavior linked to cognitive disabilities can be mistaken for willful nonadherence or lack of motivation. Reduced stamina can look like laziness, memory problems can look like not caring, and impaired judgment can look like rebellion. A person may also say they understand more than they do, to avoid embarrassment. When a person with a disability keeps missing appointments or breaking program rules, ask whether the program fits them before concluding they are not ready.

Disability services staff are well placed to notice these gaps. This course does not qualify staff to diagnose a substance use disorder, determine clinical need or direct treatment. Staff who hold a clinical credential still act within their professional role and applicable procedures. You can notice when substance use is affecting a person's goals, ask whether they want help, and help them raise the access needs they want addressed. Confirm authorization before sharing health or disability information, including during an initial referral call. Treat evidence on prevalence as a reason to be alert, not as a prediction about any one person.
lessons.keyPoint: The 2019 advisory identifies treatment-access barriers and differences in population-level rates. Examine the person’s actual needs without predicting a disorder, motivation or treatment outcome from disability.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Lucia is a care coordinator for Andre, who uses a wheelchair after a spinal cord injury and receives waiver services. Andre tells her he has been drinking more to manage pain and loneliness and wants to cut back. The first outpatient program she calls says its groups meet on a second floor with no elevator, and the intake worker suggests Andre wait until a spot opens in a program across the county, three months away.
lessons.question: What should Lucia do next?
choices: Tell Andre to wait for the other program because the first one cannot serve him.
Suggest Andre try to manage on his own until something opens up.
Ask the first program how it can meet Andre's access needs, such as an accessible location or alternative format, and at the same time look for other accessible programs so Andre is not left waiting.
feedback: Accepting a three-month wait because of a physical barrier leaves Andre without help at the moment he asked for it. Programs often have a responsibility to meet access needs, and the question should at least be asked.
Andre has asked for help. Sending him away to manage alone ignores his request and the risks of increasing alcohol use.

This is the strongest response. It investigates access options with Andre while checking other available services. Confirm availability and appropriate clinical follow-up; an inquiry does not guarantee timely admission.
lessons.reflection: When someone you serve has struggled to stay in a program, what explanations came to mind first? What other explanations were possible?
lessons.action: Choose one substance use treatment program you refer people to and find out how it handles access requests for mobility, sensory and cognitive disabilities. Note what you learn for your team.

check.question: According to SAMHSA's advisory, how might behavior linked to a cognitive disability be misread in treatment?
check.correct: As willful nonadherence or lack of motivation.
wrong: As evidence that the person has no substance use disorder.
As a sign the person needs a more restrictive setting.
check.feedback: The advisory warns that cognitive barriers can be mistaken for poor motivation. Ask what the person is experiencing and have qualified staff consider the possibilities; missed appointments alone do not establish disability, motivation or an appropriate discharge decision.

lessons.title: Accessible treatment and Minnesota's substance use disorder system
objectives: Explain the general obligation of treatment programs to provide equal access for people with disabilities.
Identify the comprehensive assessment and Behavioral Health Fund as parts of Minnesota's treatment pathway.
Plan how to help a person request access supports at intake.
Distinguish questions staff can answer from questions to route to legal counsel or civil rights offices.
lessons.teaching:
Disability rights laws include the ADA and Section 504. These laws generally require equal access to treatment programs for people with disabilities, with limited exceptions. SAMHSA's advisory says clients may not know what access supports programs can provide. They may also be unaware of programs' legal duties, so they do not ask. It recommends explaining available access supports to each potential client at first contact. Staff should give examples and act on requests. It also recommends a client pathway analysis. This means walking through each step of a program to find access barriers. Involve people with disabilities and groups such as Centers for Independent Living.

Disability protections depend on the applicable law and circumstances. DOJ guidance distinguishes prescribed medication for opioid use disorder from current illegal drug use. Current illegal use does not itself permit denial of health or rehabilitation services to which a person is otherwise entitled. Treatment programs can still have rules about illegal use while taking part. A blanket ban on prescribed treatment medication can violate the ADA. Route a possible denial to the responsible civil-rights or legal staff without delaying appropriate care.

Minnesota’s July 2026 provider manual distinguishes assessment, service coverage and funding eligibility. A comprehensive assessment informs clinical eligibility and level of care. Certain licensed facilities may begin covered services before the assessment is complete. They must finish it within the required timeframe. This exception does not apply to every provider or service. The manual separately describes outpatient and residential treatment, withdrawal management, coordination and peer support. Coverage and access still depend on the service, provider and person’s program. For managed care, check the health plan’s process.

People without Medicaid who need treatment may qualify for the Behavioral Health Fund. The county or Tribe determines financial eligibility; clinical eligibility is established through a comprehensive assessment, subject to the manual’s withdrawal-management exceptions. Help the person identify the appropriate assessment, coverage and referral contacts rather than promising payment or a placement. Use the current manual and responsible program staff when the situation is unclear.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask about usable communication and access supports, then check assessment and coverage requirements separately. For the Behavioral Health Fund, county or Tribal financial eligibility and the clinical assessment have distinct roles.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Hamid, a lead agency case manager, supports Grace, who is Deaf and uses American Sign Language. Grace has asked for help with her methamphetamine use. The residential program Grace chose tells Hamid it can offer group counseling in English only and suggests Grace read the workbook on her own. Grace has Medical Assistance and has already scheduled her comprehensive assessment with an assessor who says an interpreter will be provided.
lessons.question: What should Hamid do next?
choices: Tell Grace this program will not work and look only for Deaf-specific programs, even if none have openings.

With Grace’s agreement, help her request effective communication, including qualified interpreters and usable materials. Document the request through an accessible process and route an unresolved refusal to the responsible supervisor or civil-rights staff.
Suggest Grace bring a family member to interpret during groups.
feedback: A specialized program may be a good option, but ruling out Grace's choice without asking the program to meet her needs gives up on her preference and on the program's obligations.

This is the strongest response. It supports Grace’s chosen communication method and documents what the program will provide. Do not make a written request a new barrier; ask the program to respond through a process Grace can use.

Family members are generally not appropriate interpreters for treatment, where privacy and accuracy matter. Effective communication usually calls for qualified interpreters, and the program, not Grace, is responsible for arranging them.
lessons.reflection: If you were starting treatment and needed an accommodation, what would make it easier to ask for it?
lessons.action: Using Grace’s fictional case, draft an access inquiry that does not identify a real person. Separate general questions about program accessibility from information that would require consent or another lawful basis to share.

check.question: In Minnesota, how can a person without Medical Assistance or MinnesotaCare get publicly funded substance use disorder treatment?
check.correct: They may qualify for the Behavioral Health Fund: the county or Tribe determines financial eligibility, and a comprehensive assessment establishes clinical eligibility, subject to applicable exceptions.
wrong: They must wait until they qualify for Medical Assistance.
They can only use private insurance or pay out of pocket.
check.feedback: The current provider manual separates financial eligibility, determined by the county or Tribe, from clinical eligibility through assessment. Withdrawal-management exceptions and the person’s coverage matter; neither a referral nor a diagnosis alone guarantees payment.

lessons.title: Brain injury, cognitive disability and substance use
objectives: Describe the two-way relationship between traumatic brain injury and substance use.
Identify treatment adaptations that help people with cognitive disabilities succeed.
Explain why cognitive screening in treatment should be voluntary and purpose-driven.
Plan supports a case manager can add to help a person stay in treatment.
lessons.teaching:
Brain injury and substance use are closely linked. The Ohio Valley Center for Brain Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation notes that many people who have a traumatic brain injury had a substance use problem before the injury, and that others develop problems after it. People hospitalized for brain injury tend to drink more heavily than their peers. SAMHSA's advisory adds that people with brain injury, fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, autism and other conditions that affect thinking make up a significant share of people in substance use treatment, even when their disability is not documented.

That matters because standard treatment asks a lot of memory, attention, reading and abstract thinking. SAMHSA lists adaptations that help: appointment and activity reminders by phone call, alarm or app; simplified handouts and forms; adjusted group and individual counseling; and staff who understand that a person may say they understand more than they do. It recommends that programs offer voluntary brief cognitive screening at intake when cognitive impairment is not already documented, and explain that the purpose is to make sure treatment fits the person. The screening is a clinical task for trained providers, not something disability services staff administer.

SAMHSA also flags medication interactions. Some medications used for seizures, which people with brain injury or developmental disabilities may take, can interact with methadone. That is a question for prescribers and pharmacists, while case managers can help the person coordinate an accurate medication list through authorized channels. Do not independently advise stopping, starting or changing a medicine.

Case managers and waiver teams can do a great deal to make treatment workable. With the person's agreement, you might help set up reminders, arrange transportation that matches appointment times, share a one-page summary of how the person learns best, or connect independent living skills support with recovery goals. Keep the person in charge: ask what has helped them in the past, what has not, and who they want involved. A dropout warrants review of barriers and clinical needs; it does not prove the cause or justify blaming the person. Assess possible explanations with the person and qualified treatment staff.

Before exchanging treatment information, confirm who may receive it, for what purpose and under which authorization. Records covered by 42 CFR Part 2 have specific confidentiality requirements, with the updated rule’s compliance date of February 16, 2026. A valid consent can cover treatment, payment and health care operations, but separately maintained substance-use counseling notes require specific consent. Ask privacy staff to resolve applicability and exceptions rather than assuming that membership on a support team permits disclosure.
lessons.keyPoint: Explore access supports with the person and treatment team, then check whether they help. Keep clinical decisions with qualified staff and confirm disclosure authority before coordinating treatment information.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Nadia, a CADI waiver case manager, supports Curtis, who has a traumatic brain injury from a car crash and is in outpatient treatment for alcohol use. His counselor reports that Curtis keeps forgetting homework, arrives late and nods through groups but cannot repeat what was discussed. The counselor is considering discharging him for not engaging. Curtis tells Nadia he wants to stay but feels lost.
lessons.question: What should Nadia do next?
choices: With Curtis's consent, share with the counselor how his brain injury affects memory and learning, and work with both of them on adaptations such as reminders, simplified materials and shorter check-ins.
Agree that Curtis should be discharged and try again later.
Tell Curtis he needs to try harder and write things down.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It explores supports with Curtis and the counselor while confirming valid consent and applicable privacy requirements. Check whether the adaptations help; they do not guarantee that a particular program remains appropriate.

The case provides reasons to examine learning and access needs before drawing a conclusion about engagement. Discharge decisions require appropriate clinical review and program procedures, not an inference from forgotten work alone.
Placing the whole burden on Curtis ignores that memory problems are part of his disability. Writing things down may help, but only as part of supports the team builds with him.
lessons.reflection: What adaptations do you rely on in your own work to remember and organize information? How might that insight help you support someone else?
lessons.action: Using Curtis’s fictional case, draft a short learning-support summary without real personal information. State what the person would choose to share, which authorization would need checking and how the team would review whether the supports help.

check.question: What does SAMHSA recommend about cognitive screening at intake to substance use treatment?
check.correct: Offer brief screening on a voluntary basis, explaining that the purpose is to make treatment fit the person.
wrong: Require screening for everyone and deny admission to people who score low.
Avoid screening because it can stigmatize people.
check.feedback: SAMHSA recommends voluntary screening when cognitive impairment is not already documented, with a clear explanation of its purpose. The aim is better treatment, not exclusion.

lessons.title: Harm reduction, naloxone and stigma-free language
objectives: Explain what naloxone does and where Minnesotans can get it, according to the Minnesota Department of Health.
Describe the harm reduction approach in plain terms.
Identify stigmatizing terms and their preferred alternatives.
Draft a case note that describes substance use without labeling the person.
lessons.teaching:
Harm reduction means meeting people where they are and lowering the risks of substance use, whether or not a person is ready to stop. It sits comfortably alongside recovery: keeping someone alive and connected keeps the door to recovery open. In disability services, harm reduction can look like talking openly about safer use, making sure the person knows how to get help in an overdose, and checking the actual authority and requirements before any proposed service restriction. A local preference or an unsupported assumption about substance use is not enough.

Naloxone is a core harm reduction tool. The Minnesota Department of Health describes naloxone as a lifesaving medication that can reverse an opioid overdose in minutes. MDH describes it as harmless in another health emergency, and FDA says it generally does not cause additional harm when opioids are absent. It reverses opioid effects, not every cause of unconsciousness; it can also cause withdrawal when opioids are present. People can ask their pharmacy whether it carries naloxone, and MDH points to syringe service programs and harm reduction organizations for free naloxone. For a suspected overdose, call 911 immediately and give available naloxone according to its product instructions and emergency guidance. Its effect is temporary, so stay with the person until help arrives; further doses may be needed. Prepare through appropriate training and workplace procedures, but do not delay emergency help to resolve an administrative question. Minnesota’s Good Samaritan provisions have specific conditions and limits; they do not promise immunity from every charge or consequence.

Words shape whether people seek help. The National Institute on Drug Abuse recommends person-first language, such as a person with a substance use disorder rather than addict or user, because it shows that the person has a condition rather than is the problem. NIDA suggests in recovery or in remission instead of clean, testing positive instead of dirty, and medication treatment for opioid use disorder instead of terms that suggest medication is a crutch. NIDA notes that stigma can make people less willing to seek treatment.

Language in records matters especially, because case notes and provider reports follow people for years. A note that says a person was using again and noncompliant tells the next reader less than one that says what happened, what the person said they wanted and what support was offered. Neutral, specific wording supports accurate communication, but it does not determine service eligibility or eliminate every barrier. Preserve attributed statements and required clinical detail. Correct an existing record only through the authorized amendment process, without silently rewriting its history.
lessons.keyPoint: Harm reduction keeps people alive and connected so recovery stays possible. Know how naloxone works and where to get it, follow your agency's policy, and use person-first, neutral language in speech and records.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Kai supervises a team of case managers. Reviewing notes, Kai sees phrases like 'addict,' 'dirty UA' and 'refuses sobriety' in files for several people, including Selam, who has an intellectual disability and uses opioids. Selam's roommate recently had an overdose that was reversed with naloxone by a neighbor. Selam's provider has asked whether it should keep naloxone in the home, and staff are unsure what they are allowed to do.
lessons.question: What should Kai do next?
choices: Tell staff that language does not matter as long as services are delivered.

Coach staff on accurate, person-first wording for future notes; share current naloxone information with Selam and the provider; and clarify preparation, supplies and staff training before an emergency. Preserve existing records through authorized correction procedures.
Tell the provider to stop serving Selam until she stops using opioids.
feedback: Language in records shapes how future staff, providers and other readers see Selam and others. Stigmatizing terms can also discourage people from seeking help.

This is the strongest response. It improves future documentation and emergency preparation while respecting record integrity. During a suspected overdose, seek emergency help immediately rather than waiting for policy review.
Making services conditional on abstinence could leave Selam without support at a dangerous time, when her household has just experienced an overdose.
lessons.reflection: Which words about substance use did you learn early in life or in your career? Which ones would you now choose differently?
lessons.action: Look up where naloxone is available in the communities you serve using MDH information, and find out what your agency's policy says about naloxone for staff.

check.question: What do MDH and FDA explain about giving naloxone when an opioid overdose is suspected?
check.correct: Give available naloxone and call 911. It generally causes no additional harm when opioids are absent, but it does not treat every emergency.
wrong: It can cause a dangerous overdose of its own.
It should never be given without first confirming opioids with a test.
check.feedback: Do not wait for a test to seek emergency help. Naloxone reverses opioid effects temporarily; it can cause withdrawal when opioids are present. Follow product instructions and emergency guidance, and stay until help arrives.

cards.back: When a person has a physical, cognitive or psychiatric disability and a substance use condition at the same time. Each can affect access to treatment for the other.
The Minnesota assessment that informs the level of substance use disorder treatment a person needs, using the ASAM criteria.

Possible funding for eligible people with treatment needs who are not enrolled in Medicaid. County or Tribal financial eligibility is distinct from clinical eligibility through assessment; applicable exceptions and coverage must be checked.

An emergency medicine that temporarily reverses opioid effects. For a suspected overdose, call 911, give available naloxone according to instructions and stay until help arrives. It does not replace emergency care.
An approach that lowers the risks of substance use and keeps people alive and connected, whether or not they are ready to stop.
Wording such as a person with a substance use disorder or a person in recovery, which describes a condition rather than labeling the person.

aid.heading: Before a treatment referral
items: Ask the person what they want help with and what has worked before.
List the person's access needs: mobility, sensory, communication, cognitive and medication.
Ask general access questions first; agree with the person what needs to be shared for their referral.
Confirm valid consent or another lawful basis and applicable Part 2 requirements before sharing treatment information.

aid.heading: Supports that help people stay in treatment
items: Appointment reminders by call, text, alarm or app.
A one-page learning summary the person chooses to share.
Coordinate a medication list through authorized channels; leave medication decisions to prescribers and pharmacists.

aid.heading: Harm reduction basics
items: Know where the person can get naloxone, using MDH information.
For a suspected overdose, call 911 immediately, give available naloxone according to instructions and stay until help arrives.
Prepare supplies and training under applicable procedures before an emergency; do not delay emergency help for administrative review.
Verify legal and program authority before a service restriction; do not treat abstinence as an invented eligibility condition.

aid.heading: Words to use
items: Person with a substance use disorder, not addict or user.
In recovery or in remission, not clean.
Medication treatment for opioid use disorder, not a crutch.
Describe what happened and what support was offered, not labels like noncompliant.
